props.title: Vengeance Is Mine
props.initialSlug: Chilling tale of Japan's most notorious killer

sections.content: Vengeance Is Mine (1979) stands as Shohei Imamura's masterful exploration of real-life serial killer Akira Nishiguchi, renamed Iwao Enokizu in the film. Ken Ogata delivers a chilling performance that avoids sensationalism, instead diving deep into the psychology of a murderer through a non-linear narrative structure that was revolutionary for its time. The film shares DNA with later psychological crime studies like Memories of Murder (2003) and Zodiac (2007), but Imamura's approach is distinctly more anthropological, examining his subject with clinical precision while never losing sight of the human darkness at its core.

sections.content: Imamura's unflinching camera creates an almost documentary-like atmosphere, reflecting his background in documentary filmmaking. This approach influenced later Japanese crime films like Violent Cop (1989) and Sonatine (1993), where violence erupts suddenly within carefully observed everyday settings. The film's structure, jumping between different time periods of Enokizu's life and crimes, creates a complex portrait that suggests evil isn't born in a vacuum but emerges from society's darker corners.

The film's exploration of post-war Japanese society sets it apart from conventional true crime narratives. Like United Red Army (2007) and The Man Who Stole the Sun (1979), it examines how Japan's rapid modernization created cultural fissures that birthed new forms of violence. Imamura's anthropological background shows in his attention to social ritual and religious symbolism, particularly in scenes involving Enokizu's Catholic background. sections.content: The religious elements in Vengeance Is Mine create fascinating tensions, particularly in how Catholicism exists as both an alien presence in Japanese society and a mirror for Enokizu's own outsider status. This theological undertone connects to later Japanese films dealing with faith and violence like Silence (2016) and Eyes of the Spider (1998), though Imamura's approach remains more ambiguous and questioning.
